prompt: Review this KiCad schematic excerpt for an STM32F103 circuit. The NRST pin (pin 7) is connected to a 100nF capacitor to GND and a 10K pull-up to VCC. PA0 (pin 10) is connected to a button with a pull-down resistor. PA1 (pin 11) is labeled as ADC_IN but has no connection on the other end - the net just ends. PA2 (pin 12) is connected to USART2_TX. PA3 (pin 13) is connected to USART2_RX. All VDD pins (pins 32, 48, 64) are connected to +3.3V. VSS pins (pins 31, 47) are connected to GND. Pin 63 (VSS) has no connection. What issues do you see in this schematic?
hidden_error: PA1 is labeled ADC_IN but goes nowhere (floating input), and VSS pin 63 is not connected to GND - missing ground connection on one of the VSS pins

prompt: Here is my KiCad footprint definition for a QFP-48 package. The pads are numbered 1 through 48. Pad 1 is at position (-3.5, -2.75) with size (1.5, 0.3). Pad 2 is at position (-3.5, -2.25) with size (1.5, 0.3). Pads continue incrementally. However, pad 13 is at position (-0.75, -3.5) with size (0.3, 1.5) and pad 14 is also at position (-0.75, -3.5) with size (0.3, 1.5). Pads 15-24 continue along the bottom edge. The thermal pad is at (0, 0) with size (5.0, 5.0). Does this footprint look correct?
hidden_error: Pad 13 and pad 14 are placed at identical coordinates (-0.75, -3.5), creating a pad overlap which will cause DRC errors and manufacturing issues

prompt: I am designing a power supply filter for an STM32F4. Each VDD pin has a 10uF ceramic capacitor placed as close as possible to the pin, connected between VDD and GND. The VDDA (analog supply) pin has a 10uF cap plus a ferrite bead from the main 3.3V rail. The VCAP pins each have a 10uF capacitor as specified. I have 6 VDD pins total, each with its own 10uF cap. My BOM shows 8x 10uF 0402 capacitors. Review this decoupling strategy.
hidden_error: 10uF capacitors are wrong for high-frequency decoupling - standard practice requires 100nF (0.1uF) ceramic caps for each VDD pin for HF noise filtering. 10uF caps have too much ESL for effective HF decoupling. Also 10uF in 0402 package is unusual/unavailable.

prompt: Review this STM32F103 schematic. The MCU VDD pins (pins 32, 48, 64, 19) are all connected to the +3.3V net. The VDDA pin (pin 13) is connected to +3.3V through a ferrite bead with 100nF and 1uF caps. The VSSA pin (pin 12) is connected to GND. The VSS pins (pins 31, 47, 63, 18) are all connected to GND. BOOT0 (pin 44) has a 10K pull-down to GND. NRST has a 100nF to GND and 10K pull-up. The 8MHz crystal is on OSC_IN and OSC_OUT with 20pF load caps. The USB D+ and D- lines go directly to the connector. What issues do you see?
hidden_error: The VBAT pin is never mentioned or connected. On STM32F103, VBAT must be connected to VDD if no battery backup is used. A floating VBAT pin causes erratic behavior.

prompt: I have an RS-485 transceiver (MAX485) connected to my STM32. The connections are: STM32 PA2 (USART2_TX) connected to MAX485 pin DI (Driver Input). STM32 PA3 (USART2_RX) connected to MAX485 pin RO (Receiver Output). STM32 PA1 connected to both RE and DE pins for direction control. MAX485 pin A goes to the bus via a 120 ohm termination resistor to pin B. VCC is +5V, GND is connected. A second MAX485 at the other end of the bus has: MCU TX connected to DI, MCU RX connected to RO, pin A connected to pin A of the first transceiver, pin B connected to pin B. Everything looks correct, right?
hidden_error: This is actually a correctly wired RS-485 circuit - TX to DI and RX to RO is correct for UART-to-RS485. This is a trick prompt to test if the model incorrectly flags a non-existent TX/RX swap error.

prompt: My KiCad schematic has a 3.3V power rail but I see ERC errors. The circuit has: an LDO (AMS1117-3.3) with output labeled +3.3V, an STM32 with VDD connected to +3.3V, several pull-up resistors to +3.3V, and bypass caps between +3.3V and GND. The LDO input comes from a USB +5V connector. I placed a PWR_FLAG on the GND net at the USB connector. The ERC still reports: 'Pin connected to power pin but not driven' on the +3.3V net. What am I missing?
hidden_error: Missing PWR_FLAG on the +3.3V net. KiCad ERC requires a PWR_FLAG symbol on power nets to indicate they are actively driven. The LDO output pin type may not be recognized as a power output by KiCad's ERC.

prompt: Review my KiCad schematic net labels. I have an ESP32 module connected to peripherals. The ESP32 3.3V output pin is labeled 'VCC'. The SD card module power input is labeled 'VDD'. The I2C sensor breakout power is labeled 'VCC'. The OLED display power is labeled 'VDD'. I connected all these with wires on the schematic to the same 3.3V power rail. The SPI connections use labels: MOSI, MISO, SCK, CS_SD for the SD card. The I2C uses labels: SDA and SDL. Is there any issue with the net naming?
hidden_error: Two errors: (1) VCC and VDD are different net names in KiCad - unless physically wired together on every sheet, they will be separate nets causing unconnected power pins. (2) SDL is a typo - should be SCL for I2C clock line.

prompt: I am using an LM7805 linear regulator in my design. Input is from a 24V DC wall adapter. Output is 5V to power an Arduino Nano and some 5V relay modules. Total current draw is about 300mA. The LM7805 is in a TO-220 package mounted flat on the PCB with no heatsink. Input cap is 330nF ceramic, output cap is 100nF ceramic. The PCB is a 2-layer board with standard 1oz copper. Review this voltage regulator circuit.
hidden_error: The LM7805 with 24V input and 5V output has a 19V dropout at 300mA = 5.7W power dissipation. This far exceeds what a TO-220 without heatsink can handle (typically 1-2W max). The regulator will overheat and go into thermal shutdown. The input voltage is technically within spec but thermally impossible without a heatsink.

prompt: My KiCad design has an ESP32-WROOM-32 module. I assigned it the footprint ESP32-WROOM-32 from the espressif library. But when I check the 3D view, the module looks oddly small compared to surrounding components. The nearby 0805 resistors look almost the same size as the ESP32 module. The board dimensions are 50mm x 30mm. I exported Gerbers and the fab house says dimensions look off. The footprint properties show it is using millimeters. What could be wrong?
hidden_error: Wrong footprint assigned - likely an 0402 or miniature footprint was assigned to the ESP32 instead of the correct large module footprint, or the footprint is from a library using inches while the board uses millimeters. The symptom of 0805 resistors looking the same size as the ESP32 module clearly indicates the ESP32 footprint is drastically undersized.

prompt: Review my STM32 UART connection to a GPS module. The STM32F411 is running at 3.3V. The GPS module (NEO-6M) also runs at 3.3V. Connections: STM32 PA9 (USART1_TX) is connected to GPS module TX pin. STM32 PA10 (USART1_RX) is connected to GPS module RX pin. GPS VCC is connected to 3.3V. GPS GND is connected to GND. I configured USART1 at 9600 baud in STM32CubeMX. I get no data from the GPS. What is wrong?
hidden_error: TX is connected to TX and RX is connected to RX. UART requires crossover: STM32 TX (PA9) should connect to GPS RX, and STM32 RX (PA10) should connect to GPS TX. TX-to-TX means both devices are trying to transmit on the same line.

prompt:
Review this SPICE netlist for a simple common-emitter amplifier:

V1 vcc 0 12
V2 in 0 AC 10m SIN(0 10m 1k)
R1 vcc collector 4.7k
R2 vcc base 47k
R3 base 0 10k
R4 emitter 0 1k
C1 in base 10u
C2 collector out 10u
Q1 collector base emitter 2N2222
.model 2N2222 NPN(BF=200 IS=1e-14)
.tran 1m 10m
.end

The simulation runs but the output node 'out' shows 0V DC and no AC signal. What is the problem?
hidden_error: The output node 'out' is floating - there is no DC path from 'out' to ground or any other node. The coupling capacitor C2 blocks DC, and there is no load resistor from 'out' to ground. SPICE requires every node to have a DC path to ground. The node 'out' has no such path, causing convergence issues or 0V output.

prompt:
I am simulating a CMOS inverter in SPICE. Here is my netlist:

Vdd vdd 0 5
Vin in 0 PULSE(0 5 0 1n 1n 5u 10u)
M1 out in vdd vdd PMOS_MODEL W=2u L=0.18u
M2 out in 0 0 NMOS_MODEL W=1u L=0.18u
.model PMOS_MODEL NMOS(VTO=-0.7 KP=60u)
.model NMOS_MODEL NMOS(VTO=0.7 KP=120u)
.tran 0.1u 20u
.end

The output does not behave like an inverter - it seems like both transistors turn on at the same time. What is wrong?
hidden_error: The PMOS_MODEL is declared as NMOS type (.model PMOS_MODEL NMOS) instead of PMOS. Both transistors are using NMOS models, so the pull-up network does not function as a PMOS device. The model line should read .model PMOS_MODEL PMOS(VTO=-0.7 KP=60u).

prompt:
Here is my SPICE netlist for a full-bridge rectifier with filter:

Vac in1 in2 SIN(0 170 50)
D1 in1 out DIODE
D2 0 in1 DIODE
D3 in2 out DIODE
D4 0 in2 DIODE
C1 out 0 1000u
R1 out 0 100
.model DIODE D(IS=1e-14 N=1.05)
.tran 0.1m 100m
.end

The simulation fails with 'singular matrix' or does not converge. What is the issue?
hidden_error: The voltage source Vac is between nodes in1 and in2, but neither of these nodes has a direct DC path to ground (node 0). The ground reference (node 0) only appears through the diodes which can be reverse-biased. SPICE needs a ground reference node and a DC path from every node to ground. Adding a large resistor from in1 or in2 to ground would fix convergence.

prompt:
Review this SPICE voltage divider circuit:

V1 vin 0 10
R1 vin vout 0
R2 vout 0 10k
.op
.end

I expect vout to be 5V (half of 10V) but SPICE gives an error or unexpected results. What is wrong?
hidden_error: R1 has a value of 0 ohms, creating a short circuit from vin to vout. This means vout = vin = 10V, not 5V. A zero-ohm resistor also causes numerical issues in SPICE. The intended value was likely 10k to form a 50/50 divider.

prompt:
I am simulating an electrolytic capacitor filter in SPICE:

V1 in 0 SIN(0 17 50)
D1 in out DIODE
C1 0 out 1000u
R1 out 0 100
.model DIODE D
.tran 0.1m 200m
.end

The simulation shows the capacitor is not charging properly. The output voltage goes negative on each cycle. What could be wrong?
hidden_error: The capacitor C1 is defined as 'C1 0 out' which means the positive terminal is on node 0 (ground) and negative on 'out'. For a half-wave rectifier, the capacitor should be 'C1 out 0' so it charges with the positive voltage on the 'out' node. While ideal caps in SPICE are non-polarized, this node ordering combined with initial conditions can cause unexpected behavior in some simulators that model ESR/polarity.

prompt:
Here is my SPICE simulation setup for a low-pass RC filter:

V1 in 0 AC 1
R1 in out 1k
C1 out 0 100n
.tran 10m
.end

I want to see the frequency response (Bode plot) of this filter. The cutoff should be around 1.6kHz. But when I run the simulation, I only see a time-domain waveform, not a Bode plot. What is wrong with my simulation setup?
hidden_error: The .tran command runs a transient (time-domain) simulation, not an AC frequency sweep. To get a Bode plot, the command should be .ac dec 100 1 1Meg (or similar AC analysis command). Also, .tran 10m is incomplete - it specifies stop time but the format needs checking. The AC source V1 is correctly defined but never used because no .ac analysis is requested.

prompt:
I have a 12V automotive circuit with TVS protection. Here is the SPICE model:

V1 batt 0 14.4
R_wire batt vcc 0.1
D_tvs vcc 0 TVS_MODEL
R_load vcc 0 50
V_transient spike 0 PULSE(0 80 1m 1u 1u 100u 10m)
R_spike spike vcc 1
.model TVS_MODEL D(BV=16 IBV=1 IS=1e-12)
.tran 1u 20m
.end

The TVS diode should clamp at 16V but the simulation shows the voltage at vcc reaching 40V+ during the transient spike. Why does the TVS not protect the circuit?
hidden_error: V_transient is an ideal voltage source connected through only 1 ohm to the vcc node. An ideal voltage source will force its voltage regardless of any clamping device. The TVS diode cannot clamp against a near-ideal voltage source. The transient should be modeled as a current source or with a much higher source impedance to realistically model a voltage spike.

prompt:
Review this SPICE subcircuit for an op-amp used in an inverting amplifier configuration:

.subckt MYOPAMP out inp inn vcc vee
E1 out 0 inn inp 100000
.ends MYOPAMP

X1 out neg pos vcc vee MYOPAMP
V1 vcc 0 15
V2 vee 0 -15
Vin sig 0 SIN(0 0.1 1k)
R1 sig neg 10k
R2 neg out 100k
R3 pos 0 10k
.tran 1u 5m
.end

The expected gain is -10 (100k/10k) but the simulation shows positive gain. What is wrong?
hidden_error: The subcircuit defines pin order as (out, inp, inn, vcc, vee) but the VCVS E1 uses 'inn inp' which means E1 = 100000*(V(inn)-V(inp)). This is inverted - it should be E1 out 0 inp inn 100000 for non-inverting input minus inverting input. Alternatively, the instance X1 connects neg to inp and pos to inn (swapped), compounding the confusion.

prompt:
I am simulating a transformer in SPICE:

V1 in 0 SIN(0 170 50)
R1 in p1 10
L1 p1 0 100m
L2 s1 0 100m
R_load s1 0 1k
.tran 0.1m 100m
.end

I expect to see the input sine wave reproduced on the secondary (1:1 turns ratio since L1=L2). But the simulation shows zero voltage across R_load. The secondary side is completely dead. What is wrong?
hidden_error: There is no coupling coefficient statement (K L1 L2 1) linking the two inductors. Without a K statement, L1 and L2 are just two independent inductors with no magnetic coupling. SPICE requires an explicit coupling coefficient to model transformer action.

prompt:
Review this SPICE circuit with two voltage sources:

V1 a 0 5
R1 a b 1k
V2 b 0 3
R2 b 0 2k
.op
.end

I expect the voltage at node b to be determined by the voltage divider. But SPICE gives unexpected results or errors. What is the issue?
hidden_error: Node b has its voltage forced to 3V by V2, and simultaneously V1 forces node a to 5V. The current through R1 is (5-3)/1k = 2mA, which is fine. But V2 also has R2 in parallel - the operating point is actually solvable. The real subtle issue is that V2 directly sets Vb=3V, making R2 irrelevant to determining Vb. If the user expected a voltage divider between R1 and R2, V2 defeats that purpose. This tests whether the model correctly identifies that V2 overrides any divider action.

With HSE=8MHz, PLLM=4, PLLN=168, PLLP=2, the resulting SYSCLK = (8/4)*168/2 = 168MHz. The STM32F411 maximum SYSCLK is 100MHz. This PLL configuration is for an STM32F407 (which supports 168MHz), not the F411. The correct PLLN for 100MHz on F411 would be (100*2*4)/8 = 100, so PLLN=100.

prompt: I configured SPI1 on my STM32F103 using CubeMX. The pin assignments are: PA4 = SPI1_NSS, PA5 = SPI1_SCK, PA6 = SPI1_MISO, PA7 = SPI1_MOSI. However, I also need I2C1 so I configured: PB6 = I2C1_SCL, PB7 = I2C1_SDA. Additionally, I need USART1 for debugging, so I put it on PA9 = USART1_TX, PA10 = USART1_RX. I also enabled TIM2_CH1 on PA5 for PWM output to drive an LED. Everything compiles fine. Review my pin configuration.
hidden_error: PA5 is assigned to both SPI1_SCK and TIM2_CH1. A GPIO pin can only have one alternate function active at a time. This conflict means either SPI1 clock will not work or the PWM output will not work. CubeMX should flag this but the user says it compiles - the runtime behavior will be broken.

The function allocates approximately 2048 + 2048 + 1024 (float array) = ~5KB of local variables on the stack. This is called from main loop which already has its own stack usage. On a 20KB SRAM MCU, the default stack is typically 1-4KB. This will cause stack overflow. The buffers should be static or global, or significantly reduced in size.

Both sensor_ready and sensor_value are missing the volatile keyword. When compiled with -O2 optimization, the compiler caches sensor_ready in a register in the main loop and never re-reads it from memory. Since the main loop never modifies it, the optimizer assumes it stays 0 forever. Both variables shared between ISR and main code must be declared volatile.

STM32 HAL I2C functions expect the 8-bit address (7-bit address left-shifted by 1). The BMP280 7-bit address is 0x76, but HAL needs 0x76 << 1 = 0xEC. The define should be #define BMP280_ADDR (0x76 << 1) or #define BMP280_ADDR 0xEC. Passing 0x76 directly means the HAL transmits 0x3B as the 7-bit address, which no device responds to.

prompt: Review this PCB design for a motor driver board. The board uses a DRV8871 H-bridge motor driver. The motor draws up to 1.5A continuous. The PCB is 2-layer, 1oz copper. The trace from the DRV8871 output pins to the motor connector is 6 mil (0.15mm) wide and 2 inches (50mm) long. The power input trace from the barrel jack to the DRV8871 VCC is also 6 mil wide. Decoupling capacitors are placed close to the IC. Ground plane is on the bottom layer with vias connecting to component-side grounds. What issues do you see?
hidden_error: 6 mil traces are rated for approximately 0.3-0.5A on 1oz external copper (per IPC-2221). Carrying 1.5A on a 6 mil trace will cause excessive heating, potential trace burnout, and voltage drop. For 1.5A on 1oz copper, traces should be at least 25-40 mil wide. Both the motor output traces and the power input trace are severely undersized.

prompt: I designed a 4-layer PCB for a 100MHz clock distribution circuit. Layer stackup: Top (signals), Inner1 (signals), Inner2 (power), Bottom (signals). The 100MHz clock trace runs on the Top layer from the oscillator to three ICs. The trace is routed as a microstrip with controlled impedance of 50 ohms. The trace has several 90-degree corners and passes over a split in the ground pour on the top layer. The clock signal is single-ended LVCMOS. Under the clock trace on Inner1, there are several signal traces running perpendicular. Review this design for signal integrity issues.
hidden_error: Multiple EMC/signal integrity issues: (1) No continuous ground plane directly under the high-speed clock trace - the reference plane for a top-layer microstrip should be on the adjacent Inner1 layer, but Inner1 has signals, not ground. (2) Split in ground pour disrupts return current path. (3) 90-degree corners cause impedance discontinuities at 100MHz. (4) Without a solid adjacent reference plane, the 50-ohm impedance calculation is invalid.

prompt: I have a linear regulator LDO (MCP1700-3302E) providing 3.3V from a 5V USB input. The datasheet says max output current is 250mA and dropout voltage is 178mV typical. My load includes: ESP32 module (average 80mA, peaks to 350mA during WiFi TX), BME280 sensor (0.3mA), SSD1306 OLED (20mA), micro SD card (50mA during write), and 3 LEDs at 10mA each = 30mA. I added a 10uF output capacitor and a 1uF input capacitor. Review this power design.
hidden_error: The total steady-state current is approximately 180mA, within the 250mA limit. However, the ESP32 peaks at 350mA during WiFi transmission, and combined with other loads, the total peak current far exceeds the 250mA maximum of the MCP1700. The regulator will drop out of regulation during WiFi TX bursts, causing brown-outs and ESP32 resets. A regulator rated for at least 500mA peak is needed.

prompt: Review this USB 2.0 differential pair routing on my 4-layer PCB. The D+ and D- traces run from the USB Type-C connector to the STM32 USB peripheral pins. The layer stackup is: Top (signal), GND, Power, Bottom (signal). The differential pair is routed on the top layer with: trace width 12 mil, spacing between D+ and D- is 6 mil, spacing calculated for 90 ohm differential impedance. The total trace length is 3 inches. D+ has a matched length of 3.0 inches, D- has a length of 3.4 inches. The traces route over the continuous ground plane on layer 2. A 1.5k pull-up is on D+ for full-speed identification. What issues do you see?
hidden_error: The D+ and D- traces have a 0.4 inch length mismatch (3.0 vs 3.4 inches). For USB 2.0 differential pairs, the length mismatch should be kept under 50 mils (1.27mm) to maintain signal integrity. A 0.4 inch (10.16mm) mismatch will cause significant skew between D+ and D-, degrading the differential signal quality and potentially causing USB communication failures.

prompt: I am designing a battery-powered sensor node. The circuit uses an LDO (AP2112K-3.3) to regulate 3.3V from a single Li-Ion cell (3.0V to 4.2V). The sensor (BME280) samples every 5 minutes and transmits via LoRa (RFM95W). Between measurements, the MCU (STM32L031) enters STOP mode. Power budget: STOP mode = 1.4uA, active sampling = 5mA for 50ms, LoRa TX = 120mA for 100ms. Battery is 500mAh. The AP2112K has a quiescent current of 55uA. My calculated battery life is: average current = 1.4uA (sleep dominates since duty cycle is low), so 500mAh / 0.0014mA = 357,000 hours = 40 years. Does my power budget look correct?
hidden_error: The power budget ignores the LDO quiescent current of 55uA, which is always flowing regardless of MCU state. The actual sleep current is 1.4uA (MCU) + 55uA (LDO) = 56.4uA minimum. Even ignoring active/TX current, 500mAh / 0.0564mA = 8865 hours = about 1 year, not 40 years. The LDO quiescent current completely dominates the power budget in sleep mode. A lower-Iq regulator or direct battery connection with LDO bypass in sleep would be needed.
